Ad Astra is a cooperative 2D space-mission game for one to four players that teaches real rocket science by making you fly it. Each player takes one of four roles (Science, Commerce, Engineering or Flight) and no one can finish a mission alone: one buys parts on a budget, one assembles the rocket, one runs the experiments, one pilots every burn and landing by hand.

The physics is real where it matters. Delta-v comes from the rocket equation, transfers are computed from actual planetary data, and a design that works for the Moon fails on Mars for reasons players can discover. When a mission fails, the game explains why and lets the team redesign and fly again.

Across three missions, from the far side of the Moon to a colony on Mars, players learn orbital mechanics as trade-offs they made themselves. It matters because space exploration is a team effort between very different specialties, and the game lets students experience that directly, in a browser, on any device.
details:
Ad Astra is a cooperative 2D space-mission game for one to four players that teaches real rocket science by making you fly it.

What it does. Players join a room with a four-letter code and are each dealt one of four roles: Science, Commerce, Engineering or Flight. Nobody can finish a mission alone in their role. Commerce buys parts on a budget, Engineering assembles the rocket piece by piece, Science prepares instruments and experiments, and Flight pilots every burn and landing by hand. Players walk their characters through shared spaces (a station, a ship, the Moon, Mars) and do their jobs with their hands: carrying cargo, wiring panels, calibrating instruments, flying.

The campaign follows a legend carved in the ruins of Aztlán across three missions:

Dark Side of the Moon: build a rocket, land on the far side, find the Prism and bring it home.

Life on Mars: an interplanetary trip, atmospheric entry and landing, then a cooperative experiment that must be held together through a dust storm until the legendary red lightning and blue flash wake the Prism.

Across the Universe: Project NOAH. The team splits limited resources among four arks (John, Ringo, George and Paul), builds and launches them, leads the fleet to Mars and founds a colony where each ark contributes its part.

A Sandbox mode gives a single player unlimited credits to build anything and test-fly it. Money is unlimited there; physics is not.

How it works. The physics is real where it matters. Delta-v comes from the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, transfers are Hohmann orbits computed from actual planetary data, and thrust-to-weight decides whether you leave the ground. The moon rocket does not work for Mars, and players find out why. Where we use game values (prices, part failures, loss estimates), the game says so instead of presenting them as fact. The server is the single source of truth: it validates every action by role and keeps hidden information, such as the true quality of black-market parts, off the players’ machines.

Benefits and intended impact. Players learn why rockets have stages, why fuel for the return trip has to leave Earth with you, and why a cheap part can cost the mission. When a mission fails, the game explains what went wrong and lets the team redesign and fly again. We want students to come away understanding orbital mechanics as a set of trade-offs they made themselves, and understanding that space missions succeed through cooperation between very different specialties.

Tools. Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step; Node.js and Socket.IO for real-time multiplayer; the Canvas API for the world, the rocket builder and the minigames; generated audio for music and effects. Type checking uses JSDoc with the TypeScript compiler. More than 440 automated checks play whole missions with fixed seeds. We developed it with Claude Code as a programming assistant.

Creativity. The look is risograph print: a few inks on paper, halftone shading, slightly misregistered outlines. The logo, the characters and the menu art are hand-drawn by the team. The story mixes an invented Mesoamerican legend with real mission design, and the music references in the mission and ark names are deliberate.

What we considered. Every role needed real work at every stage, so nobody waits. The game had to be playable alone, with roles left open for whoever is there. It had to work on phones, with multi-touch controls. It had to survive dropped connections, since players rejoin their seat. We added accessibility options for reduced motion, text size and effects. And we held to one rule on honesty: never present an invented number as a real one.
